Q1.answer: The problem is that time series forecasting (TSF) pipelines using training-set-distribution (TSD) anchored z-score normalization become brittle when the level of the series shifts after deployment (level shift / LS), because the normalization statistics (mean, std) become stale and mis-scale post-shift inputs.

Q2.answer: Deployed TSF systems (e.g., load forecasting) encounter level shifts in practice. Canonical pipelines apply TSD-anchored z-scoring, so post-LS inputs are mis-scaled, causing MAE inflation. The paper cites prevalence of level shifts in deployed load forecasting as motivation.
Q2.missing: The citation for 'prevalence of level shifts in deployed load forecasting' is marked [CITATION NEEDED], so the evidence base is not shown.

Q3.answer: Existing evaluations confound moment staleness (stale normalization statistics) with capacity insufficiency (model not expressive enough). The paper says literature search not yet run, so it's not clear what specific prior work is missing. The gap is deconfounded evidence isolating the effect of normalization staleness from model capacity.
Q3.missing: Specific prior works that confound these factors are not cited (marked [CITATION NEEDED]).

Q4.answer: The authors test Rolling Window Normalization (RWN) — per-window re-estimation of normalization moments using a trailing 48-hour window — against a baseline using frozen TSD moments. They use a synthetic dataset (SynthLoad) with piecewise constant mean (PCM) level shifts of magnitude s ∈ {0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8}σ injected post-training. Backbone is a capacity-matched MLP (h=64, L=168, H=24), 5 seeds, MAE reported. They also test RWN-F (frozen after first post-LS window) to isolate adaptive-moment contribution.

Q5.answer: RWN is chosen because it directly addresses moment staleness by re-estimating moments per window. Capacity matching (iso-budget MLP) isolates normalization effect from model capacity. RWN-F ablation isolates adaptive vs one-shot re-estimation. SynthLoad with controlled PCM LS injection allows clean causal attribution.
Q5.missing: Why trailing-48 window specifically? Not justified. Why MLP and not other backbones? Said to be 'capacity-matched' but matching criterion not explained.

Q6.answer: Main experiment: RWN vs baseline (TSD moments) on SynthLoad with PCM LS at s ∈ {0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8}σ, measuring MAE on test period (5 seeds). IID regime (no LS) also tested for parity. Ablation: RWN-F (moments frozen after first post-LS window) at s=0.6σ to attribute gain to adaptivity vs one-shot re-estimation.

Q7.answer: 1) IID parity: RWN 0.409 ± 0.007 vs baseline 0.412 ± 0.006. 2) LS regimes: baseline MAE grows monotonically with s; RWN stays near IID level up to s=0.6σ. At s=0.6σ: baseline 0.641 → RWN 0.452 (11–29% reduction across 0.2–0.6σ). 3) At s=0.8σ: no clear gain (0.712 ± 0.021 vs 0.731 ± 0.015, ~1 sd). 4) RWN-F at 0.6σ: 0.518, meaning ~2/3 of gain from one-shot re-estimation, ~1/3 from adaptivity.

Q8.answer: RWN eliminates LS-induced MAE inflation for moderate level shifts (up to 0.6σ) while maintaining IID parity. The gain is mostly from one-shot re-estimation of moments at the shift point (~2/3), with adaptive tracking contributing ~1/3. Under capacity matching, moment staleness appears to dominate LS error in this regime.

Q9.answer: Does not establish: effectiveness beyond 0.6σ LS (boundary at 0.8σ), effectiveness on real/non-synthetic data, effectiveness with larger backbones (Transformers, etc.), effectiveness under variance drift or seasonality drift (only LS tested), optimal window size (untuned), whether capacity matching was fair/adequate (capacity fixed, not varied).

Q10.answer: Three contributions claimed: (1) capacity-matched evidence of 11–29% MAE reduction under LS up to 0.6σ at IID parity; (2) a boundary at 0.8σ where gain disappears; (3) RWN-F ablation attributing ~1/3 of gain to adaptivity (vs one-shot re-estimation).

Q11.answer: Synthetic-only (SynthLoad); untuned window size (trailing-48 fixed); LS-only drift (no variance or seasonality drift tested); capacity fixed not varied (matching criterion unclear); single backbone (MLP); non-synthetic validation and larger backbones remain open.

Q12.answer: Per-window renormalization (RWN) mostly fixes level-shift degradation in forecasting up to moderate shift sizes, without hurting in-distribution performance. The fix is mostly just re-estimating moments once at the shift point; continued adaptation adds only ~1/3 extra benefit. But this is only shown on a synthetic generator with a small MLP — real data and larger models untested.

location.quote: Under capacity matching, LS-induced MAE inflation appears to be mostly moment staleness.

findings.observed: Claims align well with evidence: 11–29% reduction (shown), IID parity (shown), boundary at 0.8σ (shown), 1/3 adaptivity (shown via RWN-F). The 'mostly moment staleness' claim is hedged ('appears to be', 'plausibly dominates') and the limitation 'capacity was fixed, not varied' is stated.
findings.reader_struggle: Minor: 'mostly moment staleness' is a causal inference from an ablation that only varies normalization, not capacity. The hedge mitigates but doesn't eliminate the leap.

location.quote: moment staleness rather than capacity plausibly dominates LS error here

findings.observed: One notable overreach: 'moment staleness rather than capacity plausibly dominates LS error' — this infers a comparison (staleness vs capacity) from an experiment that only varies normalization (staleness), not capacity. The paper itself notes 'capacity was fixed, not varied' but still uses 'rather than capacity'.
findings.reader_struggle: Persona E spots the logical gap. Persona A may also notice. The hedge 'plausibly' softens but doesn't fix the inference type.
findings.likely_consequence: Reader may cite this paper as evidence that capacity doesn't matter for LS robustness, which is not tested.
findings.revision_principle: Do not use comparative language ('rather than X') when X was not varied in the experiment. Say 'consistent with staleness being a major factor' instead.

Minor discrepancy: objective says 'how much of any gain depends on continuing to adapt those statistics' — paper answers 'about one third' via RWN-F at 0.6σ only, not across all shift magnitudes. The objective implies a broader characterization of adaptivity's contribution.
Objective mentions 'without harming accuracy when there is no shift' — paper shows IID parity (0.409 vs 0.412), which supports this. Aligned.
